Question: What are the things you hate to experience when selling your house?
Answer: You can't help feeling emotional about the home you have lived in and loved. You've lavished thought and money over the decor. It's part of you in a way. They know what to say to get the sale. they don't care about the colour you painted the walls in, and if a viewer says something disparaging, they know not to defend the choice but to say how easy it would be to paint over it. Whenever I've sold houses in the past I've always gone through it thoroughly with the agent but then left it to them.

Question: What changes in British society and culture have been most striking over the past 70 years?
Answer: I'm almost 70. When I was a kid in London, everyone smoked. Really everyone, including doctors. It was slightly unusual if an adult didn't. Now the reverse is true. No one picked up after their dog. You had to watch where you were walking. Everything is cleaner now. In the past, car ownership was very aspirational. I remember, as a car-mad youngster, ruthlessly judging adults on the car they drove. No one cares much now. National Service was expected. When the Conservatives floated the idea of bringing it back at the last election…well, let's just say it wasn't a vote winner. Murderers were still being hanged. No one (apart from a few extremists) wants that again. In fact people nowadays are much more likely to show understanding and pity when someone commits a crime. Children were labelled "stupid" for having what we now know are a wide range of learning disabilities. People were very deferential. If you look at old interviews of Harold Wilson by Robin Day, they were almost grovelling compared to the more provocative techniques used now. Parents didn't challenge their children's teachers. Now it's commonplace. People went to church. Now most of the population is atheist. People were not very socially mobile in the past. You stayed in your lane. We move up and down much more now. In the past, casual racism and sexism was normal. Now it's very much frowned upon. I don't remember liking my parents' taste in music much, but my kids like mine. I can't say they play the Beatles for instance, but the see merit in them. Seventy years ago, Britain was determined to export manufactured goods at all cost. It was very keen on doing business with Europe and wanted to cooperate with our closest neighbours and markets as much as possible. Now, sadly, Britain is more isolationist. Britain was a real world power, with the remnants of an empire and huge clout in the world. That's changed dramatically. In the 1950's it wasn't very common to see someone with dark skin. Now Britain is home to a huge range of cultures that all feed in to a very diverse mix.

Question: How can one negotiate with their landlord to lower the rent? What factors should be considered when determining the percentage of reduction to ask for? How can this amount be calculated?
Answer: Offer the landlord something in return, such as maintaining and cleaning the common parts. If there is a green area, offer to keep it tidy and cut. Offer to clean the windows regularly. Offer a longer tenancy agreement to save the landlord costs of renewing the TA after a year. You have to understand that landlords are running a business. Anything you can offer to lower their costs will be of interest. Calculate the benefit to them by asking a professional company to quote on doing the work, then offer to do it for less.

Question: Do adult immigrants forget their native language after living in another country for years and raising children there?

Question: How can one cope with negative experiences while traveling abroad? Is the effort of traveling worth it if it is not enjoyable?

I have kind of done Milan where I was ripped off so simply don't need to go there again…etc, etc. I focus on what I like and what has been successful, and do more of that, and I try not to repeat mistakes. But I try to keep it in perspective…one rude Parisian isn't going to ruin France for me. Later this year I'm driving a 1967 Mustang Fastback from London to Vienna. My route is going to take in places I love in France, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland and Austria, places I've always wanted to see, and I'm sure there will be one or two incidents that don't work out too well. That will be all part of the adventure.

Question: Were British people concerned about a potential German invasion during World War II? If so, what measures did they take to prepare for it?
Answer: On the south coast of the U.K. there remain plenty of reminders of constructions designed to stall an invasion. I took this shot of "Dragons Teeth" near Poole recently. They are meant to stop tanks, or at least to channel them into killing fields. The south of England is littered with WW2 "pill box" machine gun nests. These brick and concrete bunkers were quickly erected all over the places where a landing by sea or air might conceivably occur. Beaches were guarded and mined. Cliffs were manned by lookouts and were covered in wire. So whilst no imminent invasion was ever expected, measures were taken. The public were concerned obviously, but my mother, born in London in 1920 said that she didn't ever lose sleep over it. My father, a child refugee from Vienna, did however. He had witnessed the Nazis in person and knew their zeal and ingenuity better than he knew the channel and the Royal Navy.

Question: Can you share your experience with learning foreign languages? Have you ever regretted learning one language over another, or wished you had learned more than one language?
Answer: I was taught French and German at school. I didn't get along with either terribly well although I passed adequately in French. I dropped both when I was 16. When I was 22 I moved to Germany to live. Obviously I had to learn German, and properly this time. I found that the German grammar I had been taught at school and which I thought hadn't gone in, in fact had. I found learning German in Germany at times frustrating but actually for me at least, the best way to do it. In a year I was dealing with clients in German and after five years my brother accused me of having "gone native". I've never regretted learning German for a second. It's given me great insight into German culture and made me reconsider aspects of my own. I regret not learning Spanish properly. I owned a holiday home in Tenerife for about ten years and because it was in a place where the locals all spoke good English, I didn't learn. My late wife did though and I wish I had too, not so much because I could communicate better, but more because I consider it polite and worthwhile in and of itself.

Question: What causes neighbourhoods to change over time? Is it possible for a good neighbourhood to turn bad, or for a bad neighbourhood to turn good? If so, how long does it typically take for these changes to occur?
Answer: In my lifetime great swathes of London have moved upmarket. When I lived in Clapham in south London in the 1970's it was a dump. I could afford to live there as an impoverished art student. But now it's terrific and so gentrified that a lot of quite high-earning people working in finance can't afford to live there. And it's the same for many other areas. This has happened because not nearly enough homes have been built in London, so people have moved into central but crappy areas and poured money into refurbishing run-down Victorian houses. Then the nice cafés and bars moved in and bingo, you have Islington, but minus the rats and the damp. You could argue that this is a good thing. But having a one bed flat in Lewisham (not central or very smart) costing close to £300,000 to buy or £1400 a month rent is not good. It means ordinary people like firemen, teachers, nurses etc are priced out of the market. The cost of travel in London makes that worse. London has a truly superb public transport system, but visitors are staggered at the cost.

Question: Were you popular in high school?
Answer: Yes, but also no. I was popular with a cohort of other boys but I don’t think the school establishment approved. I went to a very academic, private all boys school in the UK. However I didn’t really fit in because I wasn’t interested in sport and not in the top sets in any academic subject. The only thing that changed was that when puberty hit, I lost weight and gained focus. I wasn’t outstanding at anything except art, a subject that was not academic and therefore seen as ‘unworthy’. I was good at English but as I took art seriously, I was an anomaly. This alone made me popular with a group of slightly rebellious boys. (The school was full of factions, the sporty boys, the brainy boys, the Jewish boys, the hopeless boys…often boys were in more than one faction. I seemed to fit in none, except the ones who lived near me who also didn't identify strongly with any other group). I lived near the school and had the run of my house before my mum got home from work at about six, so my friends used to congregate for cigarettes, tea and toast after school. I really think those afternoons with my cohort of friends were the most formative aspect of school for me. They certainly gave me a loyal gaggle, several of whom I still see regularly over 50 years later. We discussed Python, music, cars, motorbikes, irregular French verbs, Shakespeare, Chaucer, Oscar Wilde and Harold Pinter a lot. We were very pretentious. The huge mystery of the opposite gender was endlessly examined, although none of us had a clue what we were taking about. One or two of my friends had sisters…older ones who didn’t acknowledge us and younger ones who were desperate for our attention. I achieved a modicum of fame when at 17, I became the boyfriend of the most stunning girl for miles around. We were a couple, and amazingly, we later married and were very happy until she died. I was quite comfortable being a square peg in a round hole at that school, because I knew I would leave there for art college and I was confident about what I wanted to do after that. About 30% of my year went to Oxbridge and the rest all went to good universities, which sounded as dreary as hell to me. I wanted to mix with common people, as the song goes. I don’t know if I was one of the ‘cool’ boys…I wasn't one of the stellar, bright ones, but I had a car, an empty house, liberal parents and a confidence that served me well in years to come.

Question: What work secret did you accidentally find out that changed everything?
Answer: I was a creative working for an excellent ad agency, but in their Frankfurt office, which was considered to be something of a backwater. I had done some work which had been noticed in London, which was the head office and probably the best creative agency in the world at the time. Anyway, they offered me a job there. It was the kind of career-forging opportunity that doesn't happen twice. Of course I was very flattered, but also terrified. Could I step up to the incredibly high levels of work they demanded? One day I was chatting to a seasoned American art director who had been sent over to round off his career in Germany before retiring. I liked him, and decided to reveal my anxiety to him. "Nick, are the people who made you this offer idiots?" He asked. ""Of course not! They are bloody genius'!" I replied. "So have faith in their judgement. If they thought you couldn't handle it, they wouldn't have made you the offer". That was reassuring. But I told that I felt I just didn't know enough yet and that this was too early in my career. "Look. In this business no one knows anything. You're being hired for your taste, not for your knowledge or experience. It's about who you are. Take the damn job or you'll regret it all your life". I took the job and was there for fifteen years. It worked out great.

Question: Can you provide some examples of advertising objectives and explain why advertisers use them? What does it mean for a campaign to have a clear set of advertising objectives?
Answer: I created this double page newspaper ad for a government body whose function was to convince people in the U.K. to conserve energy. It ran in the Financial Times, the national daily for business. That was the objective of the ad campaign. Get people thinking about saving energy. Incredible as it seems today, in the 1980's this was a new idea to a lot of people. The ad was designed to attract the attention of readers whilst still being legible itself. It was just one ad in a campaign that helped put the whole idea of energy conservation on the map. Without a clear objective, the job of a creative is terribly hard. "Sell more widgets" is an impossible brief. Creatives can only really do their job if a clear task is defined for them. In this era we used briefing forms with an area for the "Single Minded Proposition", and it really did have to be just one single thought. It's what I looked for first. I suspect that has since been superseded by other briefing methods but I'd be surprised if it has produced work that communicates as clearly.

Question: What were the reasons for Germany's defeat in World War II despite having superior weapons such as Panzer tanks and ME-109 fighters?
Answer: Imagine that you had an ideology that said left-handed people were the root of all your country’s problems. All you had to do to reach the pinnacle of your potential was to get rid of all the lefties. You devote enormous resources to this issue. and endlessly toil and moil over ambidextrous people and those who might be cunningly concealing their left-handedness. Then you start wars with pretty much anyone, because you have this right-handed purity thing, so you’re bound to win, right? It turns out what actually counts in war is not handedness, or racial purity, or any of that nonsense. The Nazis mad ideology prevented them from seeing what was actually clear to the Allies: having petrol, rubber, food, penicillin, tanks, planes and ships that can be mass produced and repaired in the field etc is what counts. Certainly the Germans had some spectacular weapons like the V2 rocket, the super-heavy Maus tank and the Messerschmitt 262 jet, but they were all costly flops, dazzling pieces of theatre that wasted valuable resources and only hastened Germany’s defeat. Btw, Churchill was a leftie.

Question: Is it common for elderly individuals to become angry and bitter? Are there any effective ways to address this issue besides giving them space?

Question: For those age 60 and older, what were your first exposures to cannabis? Not necessarily using it, but hearing about it or learning of its existence. How did that shape your perspective?

Question: Is being a ballerina or ballet dancer a financially stable career? Do dancers have time for other activities outside of dancing?
Answer: For a tiny percentage of dancers at the peak of the industry I suppose so, but most dancers have to compete for contracts on an annual basis. Unless you live and work in a big city with several ballet companies, a failure to get a new contract will mean moving home to somewhere else. My late wife danced professionally in Germany for ten years, during which time she danced for five companies in five different towns. Luckily she could drive and they were all close together (except for one) so we only moved three times. In every occasion she moved to work with a better company. Her choice. I earned more than half our joint income, and nearly all the other dancers we knew either had partners or shared accommodation. She was the only married dancer of either gender we encountered. After that, she moved into teaching which is not very well paid, and then examining for the Royal Academy of Dance. That isn't a road to riches either, but she was sent to China, Brazil, India, South Africa, the USA, Italy, Scotland, Mexico and a lot of other places for a month at a time on full expenses. The pay wasn't great, but it was fun at least. Here she is (with the hat and elephant) on tour in India. Some things money can't buy.

Question: Is sweating a reliable method for weight loss? How much does it contribute to reducing body fat percentage?
Answer: Sweating itself just means you just lose water. Water weighs 1kg per litre, so if you weigh yourself before and after going in a sauna, sure, you'll be lighter. However you'll also be thirsty, so as soon as you glug down some water, you'll put weight back on. If you do some vigorous exercise that gets a good sweat up and do it regularly over a period of time, providing you are on a balanced diet and watch portion size, you'll probably genuinely lose weight.

Question: How do landlords typically handle rent increases in leases without specified limits?
Answer: I keep up with the market. I recently increased the rent of one of my properties in central London because the managing agent advised me to. The sitting tenant didn't want to pay, so they moved out and a new tenant was found. I suspect this is fairly typical.
